conventions.convention: Distribution pairings are complex bilinear with no conjugation on test functions; regular distributions pair by the ordinary integral f*phi, and multiplication is (a u)(phi) = u(a phi), never conj(a).
The distributional derivative is the signed test transpose: <d^alpha u, phi> = (-1)^|alpha| <u, d^alpha phi>, with alpha = 0 giving the identity and one coordinate derivative carrying a minus sign.
In the complex case, convexity always means convexity for real coefficients and separation inequalities are stated for real parts (Re f < a), not for f itself.

Weak and weak-star convergence are topological convergence of nets indexed by an arbitrary nonempty directed preorder; weak and weak-star closure mean topological closure, not sequential closure, and the limit must be a specified point of the ambient space or dual.

Weak-star convergence tests only the vectors of the specified predual; a pointwise limit of bounded functionals is not identified with a member of X*, while uniqueness of a weak-star limit is equality of functions and needs no HB.

The test-function topology is the locally convex inductive limit (LF) topology, the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion D_K into D(Omega) continuous; boundedness of a test set means absorption by every zero-neighborhood, and no sequential criterion is part of the definition.
The fixed-support metric uses weights 2^(-m-1)*min(1,p_m); multiplying it by two gives the 2^(-m) convention, and this metric induces exactly the derivative-seminorm topology on D_K.

Support of a distribution is the relatively closed complement in Omega of the largest open set on which it vanishes; compactly supported means the support is a compact subset of Omega, and extension by zero across the boundary requires ambient closedness, not just relative closedness.

Order on a compact set is the least exponent m admitting a bound |u(phi)| <= C p_m(phi) on D_K (so order 0 for compacts where u vanishes); global finite order is one exponent valid on every compact with constants depending on the compact; the zero distribution has order zero.

Distribution convolution is defined only when at least one factor has compact support, through a cutoff equal to one near the compact set (supp u x supp v) cap {x + y in supp psi}; well-definedness and associativity are asserted only under that compact-factor hypothesis.

Convolution with a test, (u*phi)(x) = <u(y), phi(x-y)>, is defined on the safe domain {x : x - supp phi contained in Omega} (all of R^n for Omega = R^n), and derivatives may be moved to the test factor with a positive sign, with the reflection convention fixed as phi(x-y).

SOT is the initial topology of the maps T -> Tx in norm and WOT that of the scalar maps T -> f(Tx); no uniformity in the vector is part of either, and the implication chain norm => SOT => WOT is asserted in one direction only.

Degenerate conventions: an empty open domain gives the zero test space and the zero distribution space; an empty list of functionals/evaluations gives the whole space; X = {0} carries the unique topology; ell^p sequences are indexed from 0.

Choice principles are per-item hypotheses rather than ambient assumptions: HB for norming, separation, weak Hausdorffness and weak-star duality; Countable Choice for Lebesgue/L^1 interfaces; Dependent Choice for Baire-type uniformity; full AC for Zorn and Radon-Nikodym representation, while the LF construction, finite-order estimates, sheaf/support arguments, tensor products and compact-factor convolution are declared ZF.

load_bearing.statement: The weak topology sigma(X,X*) is the initial topology induced by all maps f: X -> K, f in X*, where the scalars have their usual topology, generated by the subbasis {f^{-1}(V)}; it is the coarsest topology making every bounded scalar-linear functional continuous and is contained in the norm topology.

For open Omega in R^n, a distribution is a continuous complex-linear map u: D(Omega) -> C with the test-function topology; the pairing <u,phi> = u(phi) is linear in both arguments with no conjugation.

The test-function topology is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of {phi : q(phi) < eps} for the seminorms q continuous on every D_K; equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion D_K -> D(Omega) continuous, and it is the LF topology, not the unrestricted final topology.

A linear map L: D(Omega) -> E to a locally convex space is continuous if and only if each restriction L|_{D_K} is continuous; the induced topology on each D_K is the prescribed one and an increasing compact exhaustion gives the same topology.

A complex-linear functional u: D(Omega) -> C is a distribution if and only if for every compact K contained in Omega there are an integer m_K >= 0 and a finite constant C_K >= 0 with |u(phi)| <= C_K p_{m_K}(phi) for all phi in D_K; the quantifiers are forall K exists (m_K,C_K) and the equivalence holds in ZF.

A weak neighborhood base at x consists of U(x;f_1,...,f_m;eps) = {y : |f_j(y-x)| < eps, 1 <= j <= m} with m = 0 allowed, and the weak topology is a locally convex vector topology with convex balanced zero neighborhoods.

A net (x_i) converges weakly to x when it converges in sigma(X,X*), equivalently when for every f in X* and eps > 0 there is i_0 with |f(x_i) - f(x)| < eps for all i >= i_0; weak closure means topological closure, not the set of limits of sequences.

For u in D'(Omega) and multi-index alpha, <d^alpha u, phi> = (-1)^|alpha| <u, d^alpha phi>; the test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism, so this produces a distribution, and alpha = 0 gives the identity.

In ZF, for compact K in Omega open there is chi in C_c^inf(Omega) with 0 <= chi <= 1 and chi = 1 on a neighborhood of K; every open cover of Omega admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member, without selecting cover labels.

Restriction of a distribution is defined by testing on zero extensions; for any open cover (U_j) of Omega, distributions u_j in D'(U_j) agreeing on every overlap glue to a unique u in D'(Omega), in ZF for an arbitrary index set.

The support is the relatively closed set Omega minus the union Z of all open sets on which u vanishes, and u restricted to Z is zero; supp u is empty if and only if u = 0, and two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of supp u have equal pairings with u.

A set B in D(Omega) is bounded (absorbed by every zero-neighborhood) if and only if there is compact K in Omega containing every support of its members and sup_{f in B} p_m(f) < infinity for each m >= 0; a convergent sequence together with its limit is bounded.

On the safe domain V = {x : x - supp phi contained in Omega}, u*phi is smooth and d^alpha(u*phi) = (d^alpha u)*phi = u*(d^alpha phi), the last expression restricted to V when its own safe domain is larger.

SOT on B(X,Y) is the initial topology of the maps T -> Tx to normed Y for x in X, and WOT is that of the scalar maps T -> f(Tx) for x in X and f in Y*; SOT convergence is ||(T_i - T)x|| -> 0 for each fixed x and WOT convergence is f(T_i x) -> f(Tx), with no uniformity in x.

concerns.concern: The example needs the closed ball to be an elementary solid region in the sense of def-elementary-solid-region before Green's identity may be applied, and it discharges this with one compressed paragraph: the eight octant patches must be checked against clause 4 of def-adapted-outward-boundary-presentation-of-a-simple-solid-region (upper/lower projected images pairwise disjoint and filling the base disc up to content zero), against the compatible-presentation content-zero overlap condition, and against the requirement that a single elementary solid region counts for the 'finite gluing' hypothesis of cor-greens-second-identity-for-glued-elementary-solid-regions. The mathematics looks right (the four open quarter discs fill the open disc up to the two diameters and the circle, all content zero), but the verification is reconstructed by the reader from a sketch rather than derived.

Step 2.1 compresses an interchange of limit and differentiation: 'its tagged sums converge uniformly, together with every target derivative, to the corresponding derivative-integral candidate ... F3 on coordinate intervals identifies these candidates as the actual derivatives, inductively'. The reader has to supply that the tagged sums of every mixed derivative converge uniformly on the parameter box, and then the alternative formula D^gamma I_eps = integral of D^gamma Phi(x - eps s, y - eps t) rho(s) sigma(t) ds dt coming from the Riemann substitution of F4, before step 3.1 can use uniform continuity to send sup|D^gamma I_eps - D^gamma Phi| to zero. The step is standard and closable in under a minute, but it is not written out.

The statement quantifies over a 'countable weak neighborhood base at zero', while step 1.1 begins 'Suppose (U_n) is a countable weak local base at zero' and later enumerates chosen finite lists 'by pairs of natural numbers, padding each finite list with zero functionals'. The reduction from a countable set of neighborhoods to a sequence indexed by N (and the coding of finite lists) is left to the reader, as is the convention for a finite base.
